source.title: Superior generalization of smaller models in the presence of significant label noise
source.authors: Yihao Xue; Kyle Whitecross; Baharan Mirzasoleiman

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper; some figures and equations are flattened, but the relevant qualitative results are described in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own experiments on how label noise affects test loss across model widths and densities. It refines the scope of label-noise generalization findings, but does not report whether models fit random labels or achieve zero training error.
record.gate_note: The study varies label-noise level and measures test loss, test accuracy, or variance. It does not report training error under random labels, test error at chance, time to fit, unstructured inputs, or learning order. Claims about those behaviors in the introduction and related work are not this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study measures generalization across model widths and densities under label noise, without reporting training fit, time to fit, or clean-versus-noisy learning order. Appendix C.4 explicitly uses the early-learning premise of V6 through ELR, but reports generalization performance rather than testing that premise. Final ascent across model width does not test V4's degradation across corrupted-label fractions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors identify final ascent across width and density under label noise, explain it through variance, and find that limited data, stronger regularization, and robust methods can amplify it. They also report generalization benefits from wider, sparser models.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies test-loss curves across width and density under synthetic or real-world label noise; it does not reproduce the original random-label fitting intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported test-loss curves vary with noise level, label-noise type, regularization strength, sample size, model width, and model density.

fits_no_version.finding: Label noise can produce a final ascent in test loss as model width increases; its occurrence depends on regularization, sample size, and noise type.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under sufficiently high label noise relative to sample size, intermediate model widths can generalize better than larger widths.

fits_no_version.finding: On Red Stanford Cars with real-world noisy labels, intermediate model density achieves lower test loss than full density.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reducing model density can improve generalization under sufficiently high label noise.

record.problems: The results relevant here are primarily presented in figures without tabulated values. The study measures test loss and accuracy under noisy labels, not training error on completely random labels or test error at chance.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were omitted. Other reported analyses concern bias/variance, robustness methods, or function-complexity measures and do not test the listed versions.

untested.parts: Zero or near-zero training error on completely random labels, chance-level test error, and fitting with unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Relative time to fit true and random labels, and convergence slowdown as label corruption increases. Fixed training budgets do not measure time to fit.
Zero training error on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs. Gaussian inputs in the ridge-regression theory do not establish this behavior.

Perfect training fit throughout the corruption range and steadily increasing test error toward chance while retaining signal and memorizing noise. The reported width-dependent test-loss curves do not establish these outcomes.
Whether weight decay, dropout, and augmentation prevent random-label fitting, and whether removing them alone makes clean-label generalization poor.
Direct comparison of learning shared clean-label patterns and memorizing noisy labels over training. ELR uses this premise, but the study does not measure that learning order.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict labels apply to V1–V6. Test accuracy results in Appendix D do not supply the missing training-fit or learning-order measurements. Appendix E measures function complexity over training, rather than clean-versus-noisy label acquisition; Appendix F proposes a connection to overfitting without establishing the listed versions.

versions.untested_parts: Whether networks fit completely random labels to zero or near-zero training error, have test error at chance, and do so without changing architecture or training hyperparameters.
Training time to fit random labels and how convergence time changes with corrupted-label fraction.
Fitting shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

The study varies label noise and measures test loss, but does not report perfect training fit, test error rising steadily toward chance, or whether the networks capture remaining signal while memorizing noise.
Whether regularization, dropout, or augmentation prevent fitting random labels, or whether their removal harms generalization on true labels.
Whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels, and whether the labels are learned differently over training.

rows.subject: two-layer ReLU networks
rows.size_stated: Width varied; specific widths are shown in Figure 6.
rows.operation_detail: Trained on MNIST with symmetric label noise at varying levels; test loss measured across widths.
rows.measure: Test loss versus width; the curve changes from double descent or monotonic decrease to final ascent as noise increases, with stronger regularization making final ascent more pronounced.
rows.value: Figure only; text states final ascent occurs above a noise threshold and stronger regularization reduces the required noise level.
rows.note: The paper describes the curve pattern in text but provides no tabulated values. This test-loss measure does not establish training fit or test error at chance.
rows.check: The version linkage is correct. Split regularization and noise conditions into separate rows. Figure 6 also includes 95% noise under λ = 0. Models use 1/20 of MNIST per training subset. Qualitative final ascent is readable, but it cannot establish any listed version.

rows.subject: ResNet34
rows.size_stated: Width varied; specific widths are shown in Figures 7 and 8.
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CIFAR-10 with symmetric or asymmetric label noise; test loss measured across widths.

conditions.value: MSE in Figure 7; CE in Figure 8
λ = 0.0005 or λ = 0.001 in Figure 7; λ = 0.0005 in Figure 8

rows.measure: Test loss versus width; stronger regularization exacerbates final ascent. Under 40% noise, the ascent is absent for symmetric noise and present for asymmetric noise.
rows.baseline: Lower noise or weaker regularization, as applicable
rows.value: Figure only; text reports the stated curve patterns and the symmetric/asymmetric difference.
rows.note: The text describes qualitative patterns, but the plotted values are not tabulated. Test loss does not establish training fit or test error at chance.
rows.check: Split loss, regularization, noise type, and noise fraction. Figure 7 also includes a clean-label condition; Figure 8 includes CIFAR-100 as well as CIFAR-10, and includes 30% asymmetric noise on CIFAR-10. The stated 40% symmetric/asymmetric contrast concerns CIFAR-10. MSE models use 1/5 of CIFAR-10 per subset, whereas Figure 8 uses full datasets.

rows.subject: ResNet34
rows.size_stated: Width varied; specific widths are shown in Figure 9.
rows.operation_detail: Trained with 60% symmetric label noise using different fractions of the training data; test loss measured across widths.
rows.measure: Test loss versus width; final ascent is reported with less data and not with larger sample sizes in the stated comparisons.
rows.value: Figure only; text states final ascent occurs with 1/20 of the original data, but not with 1/2 on MNIST or 1/5 on CIFAR-10.
rows.note: The text gives the sample-size comparison, but no numeric test-loss values. The subject assignment follows the study's description of ResNet34 on CIFAR-10; Figure 9 also includes MNIST.
rows.check: The subject is wrong for MNIST: those models are two-layer ReLU networks, while CIFAR-10 uses ResNet34. Split datasets and sample fractions. Figure 9 additionally includes MNIST at 1/6 and CIFAR-10 at 1/10. MNIST uses MSE and CIFAR-10 uses cross-entropy.

rows.subject: ViT
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CIFAR-10 with different sample sizes; test loss measured across widths.
rows.measure: Test loss versus width; final ascent occurs and is mitigated by increasing sample size.
rows.value: Figure only; text states that a larger sample size mitigates final ascent.
rows.note: The text reports the qualitative pattern; precise values are only in the figure. The measure does not establish training fit or chance-level test error.
rows.check: The version linkage is correct. Split the 20% and 50% sample conditions. Appendix C.3 specifies Adam training for 200 epochs with weight decay 0.001. Figure 20 does not specify its label-noise fraction, so that condition cannot be inferred confidently.

rows.subject: InceptionResNet-v2
rows.operation_detail: Trained on Red Stanford Cars with real-world web label noise; test loss measured across densities.

conditions.value: 30% and 70% actual noise, as described in the text

rows.measure: Test loss versus density; at the stated noise levels, lowest test loss is achieved at an intermediate density.
rows.value: Figure only; text states that lowest test loss is achieved at an intermediate density.
rows.note: The study states actual noise levels of 29.03% and 70.53% in Appendix C.1, while describing them as 30% and 70% in the results. The result concerns density and test loss, not random-label fitting.
rows.check: Split the two noise conditions and distinguish nominal dataset levels of 40% and 80% from actual noise fractions of 29.03% and 70.53%. Intermediate-density optimal test loss does not establish random-label fitting.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
